The fluid equation is not independent of the **friedmann-equations** — it follows from combining the two Friedmann relations (it is the local statement of $\nabla_\mu T^{\mu\nu}=0$).

Aromatic rings have a **quadrupole**: the sign of $Q_{zz}$ decides which charge their face attracts. Typical gas-phase energies are a few to ~20 kcal/mol depending on ring and anion, strongly attenuated in water. Geometrically the anion sits roughly on the ring axis, distinct from an edge (C–H) hydrogen bond.

DLVO theory explains why some suspensions stay dispersed and others clump by adding two competing pair potentials between charged surfaces in electrolyte: a repulsive electric-double-layer term that decays as $e^{-\kappa D}$ over the Debye length, and an attractive van der Waals term set by the Hamaker constant. Their sum has an energy barrier; a tall barrier keeps the colloid kinetically stable, and adding salt compresses the double layer, lowers the barrier, and triggers aggregation.

DLVO turns colloid stability into a competition you can tune. Raising ionic strength or counter-ion valence increases $\kappa$, compressing the double layer and shrinking $V_{\mathrm{EDL}}$ until the barrier vanishes and particles fall into the primary minimum — rapid coagulation. The salt concentration at which the barrier just disappears is the **critical coagulation concentration (CCC)**, and DLVO predicts the striking **Schulze–Hardy rule**: CCC $\propto z^{-6}$ for the counter-ion valence $z$, so a trivalent salt coagulates at roughly $(1/3)^6\approx1/700$ the concentration of a monovalent one. The theory underlies protein aggregation and crystallization, cell–cell and cell–surface adhesion, clay swelling, emulsion and foam lifetime, and water treatment (coagulant dosing). Its limits matter too: near contact and in real biology, **non-DLVO** forces — hydration/hydrophobic forces, steric/polymer-brush repulsion, ion–ion correlations for multivalent ions, and surface roughness — dominate, which is why steric stabilization (grafted polymers) is used when electrostatics alone won't hold.

\begin{aligned}\dot\sigma&=J_1X_1+J_2X_2=L_{11}X_1^2+2L_{12}X_1X_2+L_{22}X_2^2\ge0\\ X_2=0&\Rightarrow L_{11}\ge0,\qquad X_1=0\Rightarrow L_{22}\ge0\\ (2L_{12}X_2)^2-4L_{11}L_{22}X_2^2&\le0\ \Rightarrow\ |L_{12}|\le\sqrt{L_{11}L_{22}}\end{aligned}
$$

The cross coupling can never exceed the geometric mean of the direct responses.

The statements agree: dispersion supplies most of the binding magnitude, and orientation-sensitive quadrupole electrostatics picks the geometry.

$$
E_{bind}=E_{elst}+E_{exch}+E_{ind}+E_{disp},\qquad |E_{disp}|\gg|E_{elst}|,\qquad \Big|\frac{\partial E_{elst}}{\partial\theta}\Big|\gg\Big|\frac{\partial E_{disp}}{\partial\theta}\Big|
$$

Hunter-Sanders models the geometry-selecting term; SAPT reports the full breakdown. Dispersion holds the rings together and electrostatics chooses the offset or T arrangement.

The transition dipole is the dipole matrix element between two states; line intensity goes as its square, and symmetry decides when it vanishes.

$$
\mu_{fi}=\langle f|\hat\mu|i\rangle,\qquad V=-\hat\mu\cdot E,\qquad \text{rate}\propto|\mu_{fi}|^2
$$

The integral is zero unless the product of the two state symmetries and the dipole is totally symmetric, giving $\Delta v=\pm1$, Laporte $\Delta l=\pm1$ and $\Delta J=\pm1$. Forbidden lines leak in faintly through vibronic or spin-orbit terms.

The walls force $\sin kL=0$, so $E_n=n^2\pi^2\hbar^2/2mL^2$.

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\psi''&=E\psi,\qquad \psi=A\sin kx+B\cos kx,\qquad k^2=\frac{2mE}{\hbar^2}\\ \psi(0)=0&\Rightarrow B=0,\qquad \psi(L)=0\Rightarrow kL=n\pi,\ n=1,2,3,\dots\\ E_n&=\frac{n^2\pi^2\hbar^2}{2mL^2}\end{aligned}
$$

$n=0$ gives no particle. Levels spread as $n^2$ and as $1/L^2$, the confinement scaling behind quantum-dot colors.

Thomson scattering of photons off free electrons at **recombination** converts a **local temperature quadrupole** in the radiation into linear **polarization**. Because polarization is generated only during the brief window of last scattering (and needs the quadrupole that the tight photon–baryon coupling suppresses before then), the CMB is polarized at the $\sim10\%$ level of the temperature anisotropies. The pattern is decomposed into a curl-free **E-mode** part and a curl-like **B-mode** part; scalar (density) perturbations produce only E-modes, whose acoustic peaks are $90^\circ$ out of phase with the temperature **cmb-anisotropies** peaks — a stringent, largely independent confirmation of the standard model. A late-time reionization bump at low multipoles measures the optical depth $\tau$.

Two elementary charges 1 nm apart: about $56\,k_BT$ in vacuum and $0.70\,k_BT$ in water.

$$
\begin{aligned}U_{vac}&=\frac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r}=\frac{2.566\times10^{-38}}{1.113\times10^{-19}}=2.31\times10^{-19}\ \text{J}=1.44\ \text{eV}\approx56\,k_BT\\ U_{water}&=\frac{U_{vac}}{80}=2.89\times10^{-21}\ \text{J}\approx0.70\,k_BT\end{aligned}
$$

At $r=\ell_B=0.71$ nm the energy would be exactly $k_BT$.

Two salts at equal ionic strength can have opposite effects on a macromolecule, so the effect is **ion-specific**, beyond Debye–Hückel screening. Ranked by their action, ions form the **Hofmeister series**. **Kosmotropes** (small, high charge density: SO$_4^{2-}$, HPO$_4^{2-}$, F$^-$; and cations like the divalents) are strongly hydrated and **preferentially excluded** from the protein surface. Their exclusion raises the free-energy cost of exposing surface area, which by Wyman–Timasheff linkage favours the state with the smallest surface — the compact folded (or aggregated) state — so they **stabilize and salt out**. **Chaotropes** (large, low charge density: SCN$^-$, ClO$_4^-$, I$^-$, guanidinium) interact more favourably (weakly bind) with the backbone and nonpolar/charged groups, are **preferentially accumulated**, and thus **destabilize and salt in**. The **anion** ordering dominates because anions interact more strongly with the amide backbone. Salting-out obeys the empirical **Setschenow equation**, $\log(S_0/S)=K_s\,c_{\mathrm{salt}}$, linear in salt concentration.

Zeta is measured at the slip plane, past the potential drop across the Stern layer; specific adsorption of excess counter-ions can overcompensate the surface charge and flip its sign.

$$
\psi_0\to\psi_d\ \text{across the Stern layer},\qquad \zeta\approx\psi_d,\ \ |\zeta|<|\psi_0|,\qquad |\sigma_{IHP}|>|\sigma_0|\ \Rightarrow\ \operatorname{sign}\zeta=-\operatorname{sign}\psi_0
$$

Multivalent cations on a negative surface do this. Point-charge Gouy-Chapman forbids such close adsorption and cannot reproduce it.

Zeta potential sets the repulsion between particles; salt compresses the double layer, $|\zeta|$ falls below the stability threshold, and van der Waals attraction wins.

$$
\lambda_D\propto\frac1{\sqrt I},\qquad |\zeta|\gtrsim25\text{ to }30\ \text{mV}\ \Rightarrow\ \text{stable},\qquad |\zeta|=8\ \text{mV}\ \Rightarrow\ \text{aggregation}
$$

$\zeta$ is the practical dial for colloidal stability.
